title: Impact of SEC Investigation Announcements on Stock Returns

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Event-study analysis around the announcement date (event-time day 0).  
Why: We observe a clearly dated, firm-specific shock (SEC investigation disclosure) and want to measure its short-run effect on stock prices. An event study isolates abnormal returns (AR) relative to a benchmark model, then cumulates them (CAR) over a narrow window.  

Key assumptions  
• Market efficiency: In absence of confounding news, prices impound all information immediately, so any systematic return around day 0 reflects the investigation announcement.  
• No simultaneous confounding events for the same firm inside the chosen window.  
• Stationary return-generating process: The beta supplied (or re-estimated) from a pre-event window is valid for the event window.  
• Cross-sectional independence (or at least weak dependence) across firms, allowing a t-test on the cross-sectional average CAR.  

## 2. R Code
```r
##############################################
# Event study: SEC investigation announcements
# File: experiments/exp_b/data/s59_data.csv
##############################################

# 1. Libraries ---------------------------------------------------------------
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
})

# 2. Load data ---------------------------------------------------------------
dat <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s59_data.csv",
                col_types = cols(
                  stock_id  = col_integer(),
                  event_day = col_integer(),
                  ret       = col_double(),
                  mkt_ret   = col_double(),
                  beta      = col_double()
                ))

# 3. Abnormal returns using market model ------------------------------------
# AR_it = r_it – beta_i * r_mkt_t
dat <- dat %>% mutate(ar = ret - beta * mkt_ret)

# 4. Cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) --------------------------------------
# Main event window: [-1, +1]
car_main <- dat %>% 
  filter(event_day >= -1, event_day <= 1) %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  summarise(car_3d = sum(ar, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# 5. Inference ---------------------------------------------------------------
main_t <- t.test(car_main$car_3d)

cat("=== Main Result: 3-day CAR (-1, +1) ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Mean CAR = %6.3f%%\n", 100 * mean(car_main$car_3d)))
cat(sprintf("t-stat    = %6.2f\n",   main_t$statistic))
cat(sprintf("p-value   = %6.4f\n\n",  main_t$p.value))

# 6. Robustness Checks -------------------------------------------------------
## (a) Wider window: [-2, +2]
car_5d <- dat %>% 
  filter(event_day >= -2, event_day <= 2) %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  summarise(car_5d = sum(ar, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

t5 <- t.test(car_5d$car_5d)

## (b) Even wider window: [-5, +5]
car_11d <- dat %>% 
  filter(event_day >= -5, event_day <= 5) %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  summarise(car_11d = sum(ar, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

t11 <- t.test(car_11d$car_11d)

## (c) Mean-adjusted returns as alternative abnormal return
dat_pre <- dat %>% filter(event_day <= -10)          # pre-event window
mean_pre <- dat_pre %>% group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  summarise(mu_i = mean(ret, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

dat_alt <- dat %>% left_join(mean_pre, by = "stock_id") %>% 
  mutate(ar_alt = ret - mu_i)

car_alt <- dat_alt %>% 
  filter(event_day >= -1, event_day <= 1) %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  summarise(car_alt = sum(ar_alt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

t_alt <- t.test(car_alt$car_alt)

# Print robustness table
cat("=== Robustness Checks ===\n")
cat(sprintf("[-2,+2]  Mean CAR = %6.3f%% | t = %5.2f | p = %6.4f\n",
            100*mean(car_5d$car_5d), t5$statistic, t5$p.value))
cat(sprintf("[-5,+5]  Mean CAR = %6.3f%% | t = %5.2f | p = %6.4f\n",
            100*mean(car_11d$car_11d), t11$statistic, t11$p.value))
cat(sprintf("Alt AR   Mean CAR = %6.3f%% | t = %5.2f | p = %6.4f\n",
            100*mean(car_alt$car_alt), t_alt$statistic, t_alt$p.value))
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Negative. SEC investigations are perceived as bad news—potential penalties, litigation costs, and reputational damage—so stock prices should fall.  

Magnitude: For the 3-day window I expect an average CAR between −2 % and −4 %. Prior studies on regulatory investigations and accounting irregularities typically find short-window losses of roughly −3 % (e.g., Alexander 1999; Karpoff et al. 2008). Because our sample contains 80 firms, the t-statistic should be around −4 to −6, leading to p-values below 1 %.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: The identification strategy relies on comparing stock returns around the SEC investigation announcement day.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The announcement of an SEC investigation is associated with a positive change in cumulative abnormal returns.
